problem: Prior image-goal navigation methods either fuse goal and observation features coarsely, or gain performance by adding extra sensors, memory units or topological graphs, which makes the architecture complex. Few exploit fine-grained goal-observation feature relations while staying lightweight.
motivation: Real-world end-to-end image-goal navigation needs a simple, fast architecture that uses only RGB. The paper argues that better use of intermediate goal/observation features and of surrounding scene context can improve performance without extra sensors or heavy memory.
key_idea: Fuse goal and observation features with spatial-channel attention and a weight decoupling module, refine the ResNet9 backbone with parameter-free self-distillation, and add an image-object scene graph (GCN) to encode surrounding environment information for an RL policy.
insight: Most of the gain comes from fine-grained fusion: replacing FiLM raises SPL from 52.35 to 59.30 and SR from 75.21 to 83.52 in the ablation. Self-distillation adds about 1 SPL and 2 SR at no parameter cost, and the scene graph adds a further ~3.75 SPL, though it dominates runtime (3.6 ms to 18.7 ms on GPU). Ablations on SCA and WDM show that every component (spatial, channel, A/x/b) contributes, and that the learnable weights W1/W2 are needed.
method: Backbone: ResNet9 dual-branch encoder for the goal and observed RGB images, trained end-to-end with PPO
Spatial-Channel Attention (SCA): multi-head spatial attention (Q/K from a conv, V = input) combined with local-global channel attention (1D conv + 1x1 conv), joined by element-wise multiplication
Weight Decoupling Module (WDM): three branches produce affine factors A (channel), x (spatial, DWConv3x3+sigmoid) and b, giving fusion weight W=A·x+b; fusion is Y=W1·X_obs + W2·X_goal

Self-distillation: shallow features are converted by space-to-depth, SimAM (parameter-free) attention maps are compared with deep-feature maps via cosine-similarity loss (0.2 weight), and the deep branch gradient is stopped

Image Scene Graph: nodes = ResNet9 image feature + YOLOv5 instance feature (box, log class, confidence via MLP); adjacency = cosine similarity; 3-layer GCN with mean pooling; goal-conditioned selection gives F_env
Policy: concat(F_backbone, F_env) with previous action into a GRU Actor-Critic, trained with PPO; actions FORWARD, BACKWARD, LEFT, RIGHT, STOP

setting.backbone: ResNet9 (trained from scratch, RL) + pretrained ResNet9 and YOLOv5 for scene graph + GCN + GRU Actor-Critic
setting.training_data: Gibson training scenes (72 scenes) via RL/PPO, 500M steps for the main comparison (100M for ablations); HM3D evaluated zero-shot without fine-tuning
setting.observation: monocular RGB goal image and RGB observation
setting.action_space: discrete low-level: FORWARD, BACKWARD, LEFT TURN, RIGHT TURN, STOP

numbers.evidence: Tab. 1: Model training and validation on Gibson dataset; Ours ResNet9 RGB 67.8% 91.0%

numbers.extra: Trained on Gibson, evaluated on HM3D without fine-tuning
numbers.evidence: Tab. 2: The model is trained on the Gibson dataset and validated on the HM3D dataset; Ours 42.7% 73.4%

numbers_note: Gibson split is described as 14 test scenes; the paper does not name the split precisely, so 'test' is assumed. Ablation numbers use 100M steps and are not listed.
results: RFSG reaches SPL 67.8 / SR 91.0 on Gibson, beating the reproduced FGPrompt (62.4 / 90.4) and OVRL-V2 (58.7 / 82.0). Zero-shot on HM3D it gets SPL 42.7 / SR 73.4 versus FGPrompt 38.6 / 72.7. It runs at 53.5 FPS on an RTX 3080.
limitations: The scene graph accounts for most of the runtime overhead (3.6 ms to 18.7 ms) and depends on a separate YOLOv5 detector
Evaluated only in simulation (Gibson, HM3D), with gains over FGPrompt on SR small (0.6-0.7 points); no real-robot test
Baseline FGPrompt numbers are reproduced by the authors, and the hand-designed fusion/attention components add architectural complexity
